'''Kathryn Uhrich''' (born 1965) is [[Dean (education)|Dean]] of the College of Natural and Agricultural Sciences, at The [[University of California, Riverside]],<ref name="Grant">{{cite web|last1=Grant|first1=James|title=Kathryn Uhrich Named Dean of College of Natural and Agricultural Sciences|url=https://ucrtoday.ucr.edu/31818|website=Inside UCR|date=October 6, 2015}}</ref> and founder of Polymerix Corporation.<ref name="Trevor">{{cite news|last1=Trevor|first1=Greg|title=Polymer chemistry expert wins two major New Jersey awards|url=http://urwebsrv.rutgers.edu/focus/article/Polymer%20chemistry%20expert%20wins%20two%20major%20New%20Jersey%20awards/1194/|access-date=November 29, 2016|work=Rutgers Focus|date=November 3, 2003|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130040533/http://urwebsrv.rutgers.edu/focus/article/Polymer%20chemistry%20expert%20wins%20two%20major%20New%20Jersey%20awards/1194/#|archive-date=November 30, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> She has received many awards for her research and work including the ACS Buck-Whitney Award and the Sioux Award. She was a fellow at both the National Academy of Inventors and the American Chemical Society in 2014.

== Research ==

Her research mainly focuses on biodegradable polymers for use in dental and medical applications. These polymers consist of esters, amides and anhydrides, all of which are susceptible to hydrolysis, thus ensuring the breakdown of the polymer in the body's watery milieu.<ref name="Acton">{{cite book|editor-last1=Acton|editor-first1=Ashton|title=Anhydrides—Advances in Research and Application|date=2013|isbn=978-1-4816-9716-3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5NqVFGyqkn8C&pg=PA266}}</ref>

The oldest version of [[aspirin]] came from [[Hippocrates]] in the fifth century BC,<ref name="Goldberg">{{cite journal|last1=Goldberg|first1=Daniel R.|title=Aspirin: Turn of the Century Miracle Drug|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/aspirin-turn-of-the-century-miracle-drug|journal=Chemical Heritage Magazine|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] |date=Summer 2009|volume=27|issue= 2|pages=26–30|access-date=March 24, 2018}}</ref> while the latest version, PolyAspirin, comes from Uhrich's lab at Rutgers University.<ref name="ACS2005">{{cite web|title=From Willow Bark to PolyAspirin: Discovery and Invention|url=http://acs.confex.com/acs/marm05/techprogram/P16870.HTM|website=Program Listing The 37th Middle Atlantic Regional Meeting (May 22–25, 2005) New Brunswick, NJ|access-date=November 29, 2016|archive-date=February 8, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208131842/http://acs.confex.com/acs/marm05/techprogram/P16870.HTM|url-status=dead}}</ref> Polyaspirine consists of anhydrides and esters that  hydrolytically degrade into the [[active ingredient]] in aspirin (salicylic acid).  Her research was highlighted in "Aspirin: The Remarkable Story of a Wonder Drug" by Diarmuid Jeffreys.<ref name="Jeffreys">{{cite book | first=Diarmuid |last=Jeffreys | year= 2004| title= Aspirin. The Remarkable Story of a Wonder Drug | publisher= Bloomsbury Publishing|isbn=978-1-59691-816-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v9AZ76VD7ZYC&pg=PA272}}</ref> Although the polymer was originally designed for biodegradable [[Surgical suture|sutures]], PolyAspirin is now undergoing clinical trials as a material for a new type of cardiac stent. This [[biodegradable stent]] controls the inflammation effects occurring after [[angioplasty]], called [[restenosis]] and disappears when no longer needed.<ref>{{cite web|title=Three Rutgers Profs Honored for Inventions|url=https://ored.rutgers.edu/content/three-rutgers-profs-honored-inventions|access-date=November 29, 2016|website=Rutgers Office of Research and Economic Development|date=2012}}</ref><ref name="Ono">{{cite web|last1=Ono|first1=Miyu|title=A Way to the Heart with Polymers|url=https://curioussciencewriters.org/2016/01/25/a-way-to-the-heart-with-polymers/|website=Curious Science Writers|date=January 25, 2016}}</ref>

[[File:UhrichKE wiki.jpg|thumb|upright|Kathryn Uhrich at Rutgers]]

Uhrich has collaborated with Professor Michael Tchikindas in the Rutgers Food Science department to investigate PolyAspirin and other plant-based polymers as a method for prevention of [[biofilm]] formation by microbes such as ''[[Escherichia coli|E. coli]]'' and ''[[Salmonella]]'' in food.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rosenberg|first1=L.E.|last2=Carbone|first2=A.L.|last3=Römling|first3=U.|last4=Uhrich|first4=K.E.|last5=Chikindas|first5=M.L.|title=Salicylic acid-based poly(anhydride esters) for control of biofilm formation in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium|journal=Letters in Applied Microbiology|date=May 2008|volume=46|issue=5|pages=593–599|doi=10.1111/j.1472-765X.2008.02356.x|pmid=18373656|s2cid=205628108}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Michael L. Chikindas, Ph. D.|url=http://foodsci.rutgers.edu/chikindas/index.html|website=Rutgers|publisher=Department of Food Science|access-date=November 29, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130043013/http://foodsci.rutgers.edu/chikindas/index.html|archive-date=November 30, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 1997, Uhrich first patented PolyAspirin.<ref name=Polymers>{{cite web|title=Polymers vs. Pain|url=http://chemheritage.org/EducationalServices/pharm/asp/polasp.htm|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100615190353/http://chemheritage.org/EducationalServices/pharm/asp/polasp.htm|archive-date=June 15, 2010}}</ref>  All of Uhrich's inventions were originally licensed to Polymerix Corporation in 2000, to develop biodegradable polymerized drugs, and now being licensed through Rutgers. The technology includes more efficient delivery to targeted areas such as orthopedic implants, coronary stents and arthritic joints. Uhrich has at least 16 patents in the US and 160 patent applications pending worldwide,  all of which are coordinated by Rutgers OCLTT.<ref name="CV">{{cite web|title=KATHRYN ELIZABETH UHRICH|url=http://urc.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/faculty/kuhrich/Uhrich_CV_31Jul14.pdf|website=Rutgers University|access-date=November 29, 2016|archive-date=November 30, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130043110/http://urc.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/faculty/kuhrich/Uhrich_CV_31Jul14.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Uhrich's second research line is on polymeric [[micelles]]. Like soap, these polymers have a hydrophilic 'head' and a hydrophobic 'tail'. These molecules form a spherical particle in which you can pack a hydrophobic drug molecule.
Uhrich's research group investigates two general classes of nanoscale polymeric micelles: [[amphiphilic]] star-like macromolecules (ASMs) and amphiphilic scorpion-like macromolecules (AScMs); both systems facilitate drug transport. ASMs behave as unimolecular micelles, where four polymer particles are covalently bound. AScMs consist of part of the star like macromolecules, and must first aggregate to form micellar structures. Because AScMs are easier to synthesize and have similar properties, the polymers are undergoing further proof of principle research in gene delivery of [[siRNA]] and [[plasmid DNA]] with Professor Charlie Roth.<ref>{{cite web|title=Roth, Uhrich and Team Issued Patent|url=http://cbe.rutgers.edu/news/roth-uhrich-and-team-issued-patent|access-date=November 29, 2016|website=Rutgers School of Engineering|date=2016}}</ref>

Also, the anionic (negatively charged) scorpion-like molecules inhibit cellular uptake of oxidized [[Low-density lipoprotein|LDL]], the 'bad' cholesterol in the body. This type of LDL is usually incorporated in [[macrophages]], resulting in foam cell formation and formation of an atherosclerotic plaque which narrows or blocks the arteries.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Chnari|first1=Evangelia|last2=Nikitczuk|first2=Jessica S.|last3=Uhrich|first3=Kathryn E.|last4=Moghe|first4=Prabhas V.|title=Nanoscale Anionic Macromolecules Can Inhibit Cellular Uptake of Differentially Oxidized LDL|journal=Biomacromolecules|date=February 2006|volume=7|issue=2|pages=597–603|doi=10.1021/bm0506905|pmid=16471936}}</ref> Contrary to most anti-atherosclerotic drugs, the anionic polymer only targets LDL particles and not [[High density lipoprotein|HDL]] particles. The delivery of these polymeric particles is now undergoing investigation with Professor Prabhas Moghe.<ref>{{cite web|title=Novel nanotherapeutics target plaque formations in the artery, preventing rupture and debilitating heart disease|website=Translational Nanomedicine for Heart Disease|url=https://www.benefunder.com/kathryn-uhrich-prabhas-moghe}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Prof. Prabhas Moghe|url=https://moghe3.wixsite.com/rutgers/publications|website=Rutgers|access-date=November 29, 2016}}</ref>

Thirdly, her group is interested in micro-sized striped patterns of protein (such as serum [[albumin]], [[immunoglobulin G]], laminin and other [[growth factors]]) on biocompatible polymeric substrates (such as poly(methylmethacrylate) or PMMA).  These proteins promote neuron cell growth, but are not always large enough to bridge the gap caused by injury and restore function to the nerve. Thus, Uhrich investigates the optimal dimensions for promoting neuronal growth in conjugation with Professors Helen Buettner,<ref>[http://sol.rutgers.edu/staff/buettner.html Professor Helen Buettner's website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510132918/http://sol.rutgers.edu/staff/buettner.html |date=May 10, 2008 }}</ref> Martin Grumet<ref>[http://lifesci.rutgers.edu/~molbiosci/faculty/grumet.html Professor Martin Grumet's website]</ref> and David Shreiber,<ref>[http://www.rci.rutgers.edu/~shreiber/ David Shreiber's website]</ref> and the most effective patterning method to generate protein gradients.  More recently, Uhrich's group is collaborating with Professor Sally Meiners of UMDNJ to create nerve guidance conduits from biodegradable polymers.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Griffin|first1=Jeremy|last2=Delgado-Rivera|first2=Roberto|last3=Meiners|first3=Sally|last4=Uhrich|first4=Kathryn E.|title=Salicylic acid-derived poly(anhydride-ester) electrospun fibers designed for regenerating the peripheral nervous system|journal=Journal of Biomedical Materials Research Part A|date=June 1, 2011|volume=97A|issue=3|pages=230–242|doi=10.1002/jbm.a.33049|pmc=3096072|pmid=21442724}}</ref>
